basicsChecklist.title: Understand syntax before you study the framework
basicsChecklist.summary: If variables, methods, if-else blocks, loops, and classes are still shaky, do not rush into Spring.
checks: Read basic Java code without getting stuck
Distinguish methods, parameters, fields, and objects
Understand why a loop or condition behaves the way it does

basicsChecklist.title: Learn OOP through real code
basicsChecklist.summary: Do not stop at definitions. You need to see classes, interfaces, enums, and records in a real repo.
checks: Know when to use an interface
Recognize when a class is carrying too many responsibilities
Be able to extract a small piece of logic into another class

basicsChecklist.title: Read tests to learn faster
basicsChecklist.summary: Tests are the fastest way to understand what a class is expected to do.
checks: Read assertions and understand the input/output
Know which test protects which behavior
Change a small piece of code and predict which test will fail

basicsChecklist.title: Move to Spring only when Java Core is solid enough
basicsChecklist.summary: A framework helps you move faster, but it can also hide the fundamentals if your base is weak.
checks: No longer feel vague about collections and exceptions
Read plain Java service code without feeling overwhelmed

tree.title: Java Core foundation
tree.summary: This is the root of the tree. If this part is weak, you will follow frameworks in Spring or databases without understanding the core idea.

tree.title: Code-reading mindset
tree.summary: Learn to look at a flow from input to output, understand side effects, boundaries, and the responsibilities of each layer.

tree.title: Data and transactions
tree.summary: Real backend work always comes back to data. You need to understand DBs, transactions, migrations, and queries instead of only calling save.

tree.title: Web and security
tree.summary: Move from request/response flow into authentication, authorization, validation, and session/token management.

tree.title: Events and integration
tree.summary: When the system grows beyond CRUD, you will meet queues, brokers, outbox, retry logic, and idempotency.

tree.title: Operations and advanced topics
tree.summary: The end goal is not just writing code that runs, but also knowing how to observe, stabilize, and scale the system.

technologyMap.name: Maven Wrapper
technologyMap.purpose: Maven manages dependencies and the build lifecycle, and it helps the project run consistently across machines. The wrapper removes the need for a preinstalled Maven binary.
learnFor: Understand what `pom.xml` pulls into the project.
Know the build lifecycle, testing, and packaging flow.
Understand why the wrapper helps reduce environment drift
integratesWith: Used across all modules `basic`, `spring`, `notification-service`
Directly related to dependency Spring, test and packaging

technologyMap.name: Java Core
technologyMap.purpose: This is the foundation. Every technology above depends on your ability to read Java classes, interfaces, collections, exceptions, and control flow.
learnFor: Be able to read service code, tests, and utility classes.
understand object model, collection and error handling
Know which bugs come from Java itself and which come from the framework.
integratesWith: Spring Boot uses Java to organize the whole application
JPA entity, DTO, event, test are all Java classes
Messaging, security, transaction all come back to Java code

technologyMap.name: Spring Boot
technologyMap.purpose: Spring Boot helps you build a web application quickly, organize beans, controllers, services, and configuration, and integrate backend components.
learnFor: Create clear APIs and web flow
Organize controllers, services, and repositories
Take advantage of dependency injection and auto-configuration
integratesWith: Integrate Spring MVC for HTTP layer
Integrate Spring Security for auth
Integrate Spring Data JPA for DB
Integrate Actuator for observability

technologyMap.name: Profiles /.env / application.properties
technologyMap.purpose: Configuration decides which environment the app runs in, which database it uses, which features are enabled, and which secrets are loaded. This is a part beginners often skip.
learnFor: Understand why configuration should not be hard-coded into the code.
Know how to split local, dev, prod, or Postgres profiles
Know how the app reads environment variables and properties
integratesWith: Works together with Spring Boot startup
Connected to Postgres profile, security config and runtime settings
Connected to run scripts at the repo root

technologyMap.name: Spring MVC / REST API
technologyMap.purpose: This is where requests enter the system. You need to understand routes, request bodies, validation, responses, and status codes.
learnFor: Understand the request flow from the client into the app
Separate controllers from business logic
Design APIs that are easy to understand and test
integratesWith: Call into the service layer
Work together with validation and auth
Return responses from DTOs or domain responses

technologyMap.name: Spring Security + JWT
technologyMap.purpose: This part helps you understand authentication, authorization, tokens, and the session lifecycle in modern backend systems.
learnFor: Understand JWTs, access tokens, and refresh tokens
Know the difference between auth and authorization
Know how to handle refresh rotation, revocation, and reuse detection
integratesWith: Block requests at the HTTP layer
Work together with controllers and protected APIs
Rely on the token service and refresh token store

technologyMap.name: H2 / PostgreSQL / JDBC / JPA
technologyMap.purpose: Real backend systems live on data. You need to understand DBs, queries, transactions, mapping, and migrations.
learnFor: Understand JDBC and JPA abstraction
Understand transactions, rollbacks, and consistency
Know how to optimize queries and avoid N+1
integratesWith: Spring Data JPA for repository
Flyway for migration
Transaction service layer
Analytics DB and data access supporting

technologyMap.name: Request Validation
technologyMap.purpose: Validation blocks dirty input right at the entry point. This is a very real part of backend work that beginners often only skim.
learnFor: Know where an invalid request should be blocked
Reduce repeated invalid-data handling in services
Make API input errors clearer
integratesWith: Works together with controllers and request DTOs
Directly related to HTTP status codes and error responses.

technologyMap.name: Flyway
technologyMap.purpose: Flyway helps manage schema change history in a controlled way instead of manual database edits.
learnFor: Understand how a database evolves
Know how to add tables, columns, and indexes in a controlled way
Tie data changes to code versions
integratesWith: Run together with app startup
Work together with JPA entities and repositories
Directly related to safe deployment
lookAt: How services and entities depend on the schema
Compare migrations with the real data flow

technologyMap.name: Kafka
technologyMap.purpose: Kafka helps you learn event streaming, publisher/consumer flow, and asynchronous backend integration beyond CRUD.
learnFor: Understand event-driven flow
Know producers, consumer groups, and retry logic
Understand how clear an event contract needs to be
integratesWith: Used together with registration event publishing
Connected with outbox and listeners
Present on the consumer side of `notification-service`

technologyMap.name: RabbitMQ
technologyMap.purpose: RabbitMQ helps compare traditional queue models with Kafka and understand transport-specific integration.
learnFor: Understand queues, exchanges, and routing
Compare this broker with Kafka
Know which part is business logic and which part is transport glue
integratesWith: Works together with the registration event
Works together with listener and topology configuration
Connected to dead-letter and retry handling

technologyMap.name: Outbox Pattern
technologyMap.purpose: Outbox is the bridge between DB writes and event publishing, making the system more resilient when failures happen between the transaction and the broker.
learnFor: Understand consistency between the DB and events
Understand why direct publishing is fragile
Understand retry, pending, and dead-letter states
integratesWith: Connected to transaction service
Connected to Kafka and Rabbit publisher
Connected to a dispatcher that runs after commit

technologyMap.name: JUnit / Mockito / MockMvc / Testcontainers
technologyMap.purpose: Without testing, you are only guessing. Tests are the fastest way to understand code and the safety rail during refactoring.
learnFor: Understand class and endpoint behavior
Differentiate unit test, web test, integration test
Stay safe while changing code
integratesWith: MockMvc work with controller
Mockito work with service logic
Testcontainers work with a real database

technologyMap.name: Connection Pool
technologyMap.purpose: Many people study databases but forget how connections are managed. Connection pool has a big impact on performance and stability.
learnFor: Understand why you should not open a brand-new connection for every request
Understand how dangerous pool exhaustion can be
Know where to look when the database hangs or times out
integratesWith: Works together with Spring Data/JDBC
Connected to DB profile and runtime metrics
Directly affects request performance
lookAt: Tests or flows that hit the database repeatedly

technologyMap.name: Spring Actuator + Metrics
technologyMap.purpose: You need to know whether the system is healthy or in trouble. Actuator and metrics are your entry point into observability.
learnFor: Inspect health, info, and runtime metrics
Know which requests are slow and which errors are increasing
Measure before you optimize
integratesWith: Used together with the runtime dashboard
Used together with custom business observability
Connected to auth, registration, and outbox metrics

technologyMap.name: Docker Compose / Postgres profile
technologyMap.purpose: Helps you learn how to run a stack that is closer to the real world than a simple in-memory local setup.
learnFor: Understand how environment profiles work
Understand how the app connects to an external database
Know where simple local setup differs from a real environment
integratesWith: Works together with the Spring Postgres profile
Used together with migrations and integration tests
Acts as a bridge into deployment and operations thinking
lookAt: The Postgres run section in the README

integrationFlow.title: Browser / curl / test call enters the HTTP layer
integrationFlow.summary: Everything starts with the request. This is the entry point for learning controllers, validation, auth, and response design.

integrationFlow.title: Spring Security checks tokens and permissions
integrationFlow.summary: A protected request passes through the JWT filter, role checks, and security configuration before it reaches business logic.

integrationFlow.title: The controller calls the service and orchestrates the use case
integrationFlow.summary: This is where business code starts: validating rules, coordinating repositories, and attaching audit, auth context, and metrics.

integrationFlow.title: The service touches the database through JPA/JDBC and transactions
integrationFlow.summary: When the flow involves data, this is where transactions, rollbacks, Flyway schema changes, and connection pools start to matter.

integrationFlow.title: Side effects move through the outbox and broker
integrationFlow.summary: Things like notifications or downstream events do not always need to stay tightly coupled to a synchronous transaction.

integrationFlow.title: Runtime is observed through health, metrics, and profiles
integrationFlow.summary: This is the layer where you see the system as a real service: whether it is healthy, which profile it is running with, and where the bottleneck lives.

phases.title: Solidify Java Core
phases.summary: Focus on the foundation so you can read the code in `basic/` without guessing.
topics: Data types, methods, if-else blocks, loops
Basic JUnit and how to read tests
actions: Read and run the code in the `basic/` module
Open the tests first, then guess what the class is doing
Change one small method yourself and observe which tests fail or pass
outcomes: Read Java without getting stuck on syntax
Know which responsibility each class is holding
Understand the difference between OOP theory and real code

phases.title: Learn web flow with Spring Boot
phases.summary: Start with controllers, requests, responses, services, and DTOs.
actions: Read the `controller -> service -> repository` flow in the `spring/` module
Try adding one small endpoint
Write a test for the main success path and one error case
outcomes: Understand how requests enter the app in practice
Know why controllers should stay thin
Stop seeing Spring as mysterious technical magic

phases.title: Go deeper into data and transactions
phases.summary: This is the stage where you move from basic CRUD to understanding data correctness.
actions: compare code JDBC in `basic/` with JPA/JdbcTemplate in `spring/`
Read migrations in order starting from V1
Explain the rollback flow in the service yourself
outcomes: Understand how the system writes data correctly and consistently
Know why N+1 queries are dangerous
Lose the illusion that calling `save()` means the job is done

phases.title: Auth, security and session
phases.summary: This is a very valuable backend area because it touches security and system boundaries.
actions: Read the auth tests first
Trace `AuthController`, the token service, and the token store
Draw the `login -> refresh -> logout -> logout-all` flow yourself
outcomes: Understand the practical difference between access tokens and refresh tokens
Know why reuse detection matters
Stop treating auth as nothing more than successful login

phases.title: Messaging and systems thinking
phases.summary: Move from simple direct calls into architectures with events, publishers, consumers, and delay.
actions: Follow the flow from registration to the event publisher
Read the outbox store and dispatcher
Compare transport logic with business logic
outcomes: Understand why event-driven systems increase complexity
Know where event publishing can break
Start thinking like someone operating a real system

phases.title: Advanced: observability, performance, and trade-offs
phases.summary: This is the shift from someone who can build features to someone who can keep a system healthy.
actions: Read the dashboard and observability parts in `spring/`
Ask what logs or metrics each flow needs
Review code by risk, not only by style
outcomes: Know what to measure before optimizing
Know how to spot the blast radius of a change
Build advanced backend thinking instead of only stitching features together

phases.title: Design and refactor with intent
phases.summary: Learn how to make code easy to change, not just able to run today.
topics: Read code the way you would review production code
actions: Point out one overloaded class in the repo
Write a short refactor proposal
Split one flow into clearer steps
outcomes: Start thinking in terms of responsibility and boundaries
Know whether code is hard because of domain complexity or weak design
Change code with a smaller blast radius

phases.title: Senior backend mindset
phases.summary: This is the layer where you view the system through trade-offs, risk, and long-term operability.
actions: Ask what data each change affects
Write down trade-offs for difficult decisions
Evaluate endpoints from security, performance, and operations perspectives
outcomes: Stop asking only how to make it run
Know how to ask where the system will break
Read and write backend code with more mature judgment

practiceMap.focus: Do not rush straight into frameworks. The goal is to read classes, tests, and collections solidly.
doNow: Open the tests and explain each assertion

practiceMap.focus: Focus on the request flow instead of opening random files.
doNow: Follow the service down to the repository

practiceMap.focus: Compare plain Java with framework abstractions to understand what the framework is hiding.
doNow: Count how many times one request hits the database

practiceMap.focus: Do not only test successful login. Study failure paths and the session lifecycle too.
doNow: See how refresh tokens work in practice
Ask what happens if a token leaks

practiceMap.focus: Shift from direct-call thinking toward events, eventual consistency, and retry behavior.
doNow: Read the outbox first, then the broker
Ask how duplicate messages are handled
Ask what happens to the data if publishing fails

practiceMap.focus: Learn how to measure, observe, review, and optimize based on real bottlenecks.
doNow: Check the blast radius of every change
Write down trade-offs for key decisions

pitfalls.title: Studying Spring before Java Core is solid
pitfalls.why: This is the most common mistake. Learners can run the project but still do not understand what classes, objects, collections, and exceptions are doing.
mistakes: Memorize annotations but cannot read plain Java service code
Confuse Java bugs with framework bugs
Change code by trial and error
fix: Go back to the `basic/` module and read tests first
Practice collections, exceptions, and OOP with real classes
Move to Spring only when reading Java no longer feels shaky

pitfalls.title: Seeing backend as simple CRUD
pitfalls.why: Real backend work is not just reading and writing data. It also includes auth, transactions, side effects, retries, and observability.
mistakes: Only care whether the endpoint returns 200
Do not ask what happens when the data is half wrong
Ignore logs, metrics, timeouts, and blast radius
fix: Ask what happens if each flow fails halfway through
Connect your learning to data consistency and side effects
Read the auth, outbox, and metrics code too, not only the controller

pitfalls.title: Using a framework without knowing what it abstracts
pitfalls.why: Spring and JPA are convenient, but that convenience can hide SQL, transactions, proxies, lazy loading, and query cost from learners.
mistakes: Assume calling `save()` means the problem is solved
Do not count the real number of queries
Do not understand why annotations sometimes fail to behave as expected
fix: Compare JDBC in `basic/` with JPA in `spring/`
Read SQL logs, migrations, and transaction tests
Explain proxies, rollbacks, and the outbox flow in your own words

pitfalls.title: Learning technologies separately without connecting them into one system
pitfalls.why: Knowing what Kafka, JWT, or Flyway are is still not enough if you do not understand how they hook into the same backend flow.
mistakes: Do not visualize which layers a request passes through
Do not know which pain point each technology solves
fix: Use this roadmap in end-to-end flow order
Read the section about how technologies integrate together
For each technology, ask which part of the system it connects to

visualSteps.short: Syntax, OOP, collections, exceptions, strings, and basic testing.
focus: Be able to change a small method

visualSteps.title: Spring Web
visualSteps.short: Controller, service, DTO, validation, request-response flow.

visualSteps.title: Data
visualSteps.short: JDBC, SQL, JPA, transaction, migration, consistency.

visualSteps.title: Security
visualSteps.short: JWT, refresh token, role-based auth, session lifecycle.

visualSteps.title: Messaging
visualSteps.short: Outbox, Kafka, RabbitMQ, retry, dead-letter, idempotency.

visualSteps.title: Observability

visualSteps.title: Refactor
visualSteps.short: Read hard code, reduce coupling, increase clarity, and stay safe with tests.

visualSteps.title: Senior Mindset
visualSteps.short: Look at the system through data, risk, operations, and the ability to change it.
